Overview

Does gold have a pattern you can trade after costs? Instead of tuning until something looks good, this study fixed its rules first, sealed the last four years of data behind a hash, and opened it once. The answer was no. The evidence for that no is the product: a clean 1-minute dataset back to 2003, a measured cost model, and a pipeline that also runs on pure noise to show what luck looks like.

  • 23years of 1-minute data
  • 46,550rule combinations tested
  • 32walk-forward ML models
  • 9noise series used as controls

What it does

01Data you can trust

Dukascopy and broker history merged session by session, in UTC, with a report of every gap.

02Rules fixed before results

Splits, budgets, the cost model and the pass mark were written down before any model was trained.

03A sealed holdout

The final years were hashed and opened once, for four frozen candidates.

04Tested against noise

The whole pipeline ran again on nine synthetic series with no signal, to show what luck produces.

05Honest reporting

The best candidate made +0.35 R per trade on the holdout, but on 71 trades and after losing on validation. It was rejected.

06Feeds the charts

The same data powers Kakapips, and its training edition draws these strategies on real bars.

For the technical reader

How it's built

  • Python
  • pandas
  • NumPy
  • scikit-learn
  • LightGBM
  • Numba
  • MQL5
  1. A resumable, throttled downloader that caches every day as its own file.
  2. Resampling from 5 minutes to monthly, with trading days cut at 17:00 New York.
  3. Deflated Sharpe Ratio and Wilson intervals, so lucky results are called lucky.
  4. LightGBM walk-forward models and a Numba-accelerated trade simulator.
